Subject: Appliance connectivity and interconnect questions for on‑prem pilot

Hi Avery,

Thanks again for the walkthrough last week. We are preparing the internal RFP packet for the on‑prem pilot and have a few follow‑ups to make sure the network and appliance constraints are captured correctly before we move to procurement:

- Can Redwood run the private deployment via an L2 appliance (physical or virtual) that terminates into our VPC via an AWS Direct Connect/Partner Interconnect?
- What are the supported BGP/ASN behaviors and whether we require BGP sessions to be established to a specific Redwood ASN?
- Any MTU recommendations when traversing a VXLAN or Direct Connect with jumbo frames?
- Our security team requires a list of appliance firmware versions and whether we support offline (air‑gapped) activation workflows for the appliance image.
- How do you handle certificate rotation for mutual TLS between our edge appliance and Redwood control plane if the control plane is in a private VPC?

We're trying to lock the procurement spec by EOW. If you could provide short answers and any supporting diagrams or docs that would be great.

Thanks,
Alex Tanner

Alex — quick technical answers below; attaching a simplified network-diagram (network-diagram-v1.pdf) and a firmware list (appliance-firmware-list.csv).

1) L2 appliance & interconnect: We support both a physical appliance and a virtual appliance (OVA) that terminates into the customer's VPC. For AWS Direct Connect or partner circuits, the typical topology is: appliance -> customer edge -> DX/partner -> VPC. We also support transit‑VPC/Transit Gateway attachments if you prefer. The attached diagram shows three supported topologies.

2) BGP/ASN: Redwood can operate either in a shared‑ASN mode or a negotiated ASN pair. For Dedicated on‑prem peers we typically recommend customer uses their ASN and peers to Redwood's ASN (65080) via BGP session. We also support using eBGP multihop where required. If you require uniqueness we can allocate a private ASN for the session.

3) MTU guidance: When using VXLAN over Direct Connect, plan for a 50–100 byte overhead. We recommend 9000 MTU end‑to‑end where possible; otherwise set PMTU to 9000 on the appliance and verify jumbo frame propagation on the DX path. If you must transit networks that do not support jumbo frames, fall back to 1500 and enable fragmentation avoidance on the appliance.

4) Firmware / air‑gapped activation: We maintain signed appliance images and firmware versions listed in the attached CSV. For air‑gapped installations, we support an offline activation flow: we provide a signed activation blob and an installation bundle that can be transferred via secure USB. The activation requires a one‑time handshake with an HSM token at Redwood that can be executed via a temporary, customer‑initiated proxy connection or an offline signature exchange (suitable for air‑gapped environments). Documentation and attestation logs are produced locally and can be provided as artifact.

5) mTLS / certificate rotation: For control plane connectivity you can use mutual TLS with either our managed PKI or a customer‑provided CA. Certificate rotation is supported via ACME‑style API calls for automated renewal or manual rotation with bundle upload. For private control planes in a VPC, the control plane endpoints are reachable only over the peer (DX/transit) and we accept x509 bundles signed by your internal CA. We also support PKCS#11/HSM integrations for key material if your security policy mandates no exportable keys on the appliance.

Notes:
- We will need your preferred ASN and whether you plan to use Transit Gateway or direct VPC peering to provide a line‑by‑line network runbook.
- For POCs we can pre‑stage a virtual appliance image and run a 48–72 hour traffic soak to validate MTU/BGP behavior.

Happy to jump on a 30m technical call if you want to walk the diagram.

— Diego
Diego Fernandez
Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Redwood Inference

Diego — thanks for the detailed breakdown, that helps a lot. Two follow‑ups:

- For the offline activation: can you confirm the exact commands and file formats for the activation blob (we need to include them in our change window checklist)? Is the blob time‑bound?
- For certificate rotation: can you confirm whether Redwood supports our internal HashiCorp Vault CA and whether the PKCS#11 integration can use our HSM vendor (Luna HSM)?

Procurement note: we prefer the pre‑staged virtual image for the POC and will run it in our isolated staging VPC first. Please include an egress/egress‑control checklist for the POC.

Hi Alex —

Couple of procurement and runbook items for your packet:

- We can provide a standard POC statement of work (PDF) and a 30‑day trial license. I'll attach the SOW template to the Drive link and push a pre‑filled DocuSign for your review.
- Egress controls for the POC: by default the appliance will only establish outbound control connections to the Redwood control endpoints (TLS) and to our artifact repository for updates; we can enforce an allowlist of IPs and ports. We will provide an egress checklist with specific FQDNs/IPs and ports (see drive link).
- Activation blob: the offline activation artifact is a signed JSON blob and is time‑bound (default 72 hours, configurable). We can also do a manual signature exchange; details and command examples will be in the install appendix.
- Vault / HSM: we support HashiCorp Vault as a CA signer and integrate with HSM vendors that expose PKCS#11 (Luna HSM is supported). We will add a short integration appendix showing the PKCS#11 env vars and configuration snippets.

Next steps:
1) Diego will attach the simplified diagram and firmware list (done).
2) I will create a pre‑filled DocuSign SOW and a one‑page POC checklist by EOD.
3) Avery will coordinate a 30m call to validate the POC schedule with your infra team.

Thanks,
Irene Choi
Senior Solutions Manager, Redwood Inference
